title: Low Level Technicals of LLMs: Daniel Han
talk_summary: Daniel Han walks through the low-level math and PyTorch code of a Llama-style transformer (attention, RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, cross-entropy) and then shows how his team found and fixed real bugs in Gemma/Mistral reference implementations by diffing layer-by-layer outputs against the original implementation. The transferable core is a debugging methodology: compare implementations numerically, isolate components, and treat precision/upcasting choices as correctness-critical.

takeaways.technique: Layer-by-layer numerical diff against a reference implementation
takeaways.what_they_do: Run the reference implementation and the suspect implementation, capture the output of every layer, and plot log L2 error per layer to localize where they diverge.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you check each layer the output you compare it with the original imp the correct implementation and check what's the error
takeaways.numbers: Gemma has 18 layers; error plotted on log scale, each line a fix

takeaways.technique: Isolate each component and test it separately
takeaways.what_they_do: Rather than testing the whole model, they check each component (norm, RoPE, activation) in isolation against its formula, using a graphing tool to verify behavior.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you isolate each component separately and then test it

takeaways.what_they_do: They found that downcasting RoPE or norms to float16/bf16 silently corrupts results, and that implementations must match the original's upcast/downcast points exactly.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you must not downcast rope if you do you will get wrong results
takeaways.numbers: RoPE fix caused the largest error drop of all fixes

takeaways.what_they_do: They read config.json of every new model and found real bugs (EOS==pad token, sliding window 2047 not 2048, wrong context length).
takeaways.evidence_quote: always when you go to like new models always read the config file
takeaways.numbers: sliding window set to 2047 instead of 2048; pad token ID equal to EOS

takeaways.what_they_do: Explains that bf16 vs fp32 vs fp8 changes speed ~5-10x but introduces correctness risks, so precision must be chosen deliberately per component.
takeaways.evidence_quote: float 32 to float 16 is actually not two it's actually much more I think it's five

takeaways.technique: Human-in-the-loop guessing cannot be fully automated
takeaways.what_they_do: They note that deciding which of several implementations is 'correct' requires human judgment, so bug-finding can be automated but resolution needs a human arbiter.
